votemeta.desc: Adoption of the negotiated deal to approve the parking meter sale to Stonepeak Partners. A "yes" vote meant to approve the deal, and "no" vote meant to not approve the deal.

Increasing the threshold for the City Council to approve new debt and borrowing up to a three-fifths or 30-member margin from a simple 26-vote majority. A "yes" vote meant increasing the threshold to 30 members for new debt, a "no" vote meant allowing for a simple majority, 26-vote, similar to all other legislation. The mayor vetoed this after it passed in council.

votemeta.full: Allowing VGT's (Virtual Gambling Terminals) from Bars & Restaurants
votemeta.desc: This was an effort to ban virtual gambling machines within bars and restaurants – a "no" vote meant that they would be banned, and "yes" vote meant that they would be allowed.

votemeta.full: Repeal of Phase-Out of Subminimum Wage
votemeta.desc: An effort to repeal the abolition of the subminimum wage of Chicago (originally implemented as a multi-year phaseout). Yes = Repeal/Freeze the phase-out of the subminimum wage, No = Continue phasing out the subminimum wage.

In its final state – there were two options present: Option A – selling ~$900M of resident debt to a third party for a revenue of ~$90M, or Option B – implementing a per person / per month tax on large companies with more than 500 employees working in Chicago, that was projected to raise at lease $90M. This was the vote for Option A – a "yes" vote meant accepting Option A, and "no" vote meant not accepting Option A.

An ordinance championed by Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) in response to downtown 'teen takeovers,' letting the police superintendent declare a curfew anywhere in the city with 30 minutes' notice. The Council passed it 27-22 in June 2025, but Mayor Johnson vetoed it — his first veto — and the Council failed to override in July 2025. Yes = placing the power of the police to be able to creat a "snap curfew", which had constitutional challenges, No = maintaining the current ability for the police to enact curfews.

votemeta.full: Creation of Green Social Housing Across Chicago
votemeta.desc: An ordinance to create the infrastructure for the city to build and finance Green Social Housing across the city. Yes = create the infrastructure of a development corporation, No = do not create the infrastructrue for a development corporation.

votemeta.full: Reject Applicants for City Employment Convicted of January 6 Riot Participation
votemeta.desc: An ordinance to barre / reject applicants to city jobs that have been convicted of January 6 riot participation. A "yes" vote meant to barre those applicants, a "no" vote meant to not create this rule.

A series of Council actions over the city's ShotSpotter (SoundThinking) gunshot-detection contract, which Mayor Johnson moved to cancel. The Council repeatedly pushed back, voting 34-14 in May 2024 and again in September 2024 to limit the mayor's ability to end the contract. Yes = Extend the contract with SoundThinking, No = End the contract with SoundThinking

votemeta.full: Create a $1.5Bn Housing & Economic Development Bond
votemeta.desc: The creation of the largest housing and economic development bond in the history of the city. Yes = create the $1.5Bn Housing & Economic Development Bond, No = do not create the $1.5Bn Housing & Economic Development Bond

A non-binding resolution calling for a permanent ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza. Mayor Brandon Johnson cast a tie-breaking vote in favor in January 2024, making Chicago the largest U.S. city at the time to pass such a resolution. Yes = call for a permanent ceasefire, No = do not call for a ceasefire

votemeta.full: Paid Leave & Paid Sick Leave Ordinance
votemeta.desc: An ordinance requiring most Chicago employers to give workers 10 paid days off a year — five sick days and five for any reason — among the most expansive municipal paid-leave laws in the nation. The Council passed it 36-12 in November 2023; implementation was later delayed to July 2024. Yes = require these paid leave policies, No = do not require these paid leave policies

votemeta.full: Allowing for a Ballot Referendum on Bring Chicago Home
votemeta.desc: A measure to place a binding referendum on the March 2024 ballot asking voters to convert the city's flat real-estate transfer tax into a graduated tax, raising rates on property sales above $1 million to fund homelessness services. The Council voted 32-17 to put it on the ballot; voters narrowly rejected the referendum in March 2024. Yes = place this policy on the ballot for voters to decide, No = do not place this policy on the ballot for voters to decide
